passage: "You've barely touched your dinner, Jatin," Amandeep said, and sat beside his nephew on the balcony step. "Rohan and the others stopped calling you, didn't they?" Jatin shrugged. "I'll tell you about the year my own group split. I was sixteen. I stopped answering the door and wrote half-sentences on the back wall of my room, things only I understood. Then I rode my bicycle until my legs shook, every single evening." He smiled a little. "It felt like the whole world had ended. My mother never asked me to snap out of it. She left tea outside my door. A cousin dropped by and sat on my floor with me. That helped more than anything he said."

qa.q: What did Amandeep write on the back wall of his room?
qa.a: He wrote half-sentences that only he understood.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling in the year his group split?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and very sad, shown by not answering the door, riding his bicycle until his legs shook, and feeling that the whole world had ended.

qa.q: How could Jatin's family support him right now?
qa.a: They could stay nearby without hurrying him, listen when he wants to talk, and invite him for small activities, as Amandeep's mother and cousin did.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's mother have felt while leaving tea outside the door?
qa.a: She was probably worried and wanted to help, but chose to give him space and quiet care instead of pushing him to feel better. 🤍

grounding: A teen after a friend group split withdraws and throws himself into activity, and family support helps recovery.

passage: Snow fell sideways across the village court, and the power had gone out an hour ago. Dolma kept running drills on the cold ground long after the other players went home, her breath white. That morning she had changed her status to a single line: "some doors close quietly." Nobody had asked what it meant. Anirban, the goalkeeper, had seen it on his cracked phone screen, and now he stood at the edge of the court with a torch, waiting for her to notice him. When she finally stopped, he said, "I'm not asking you to explain. Want to run or sit?" Dolma looked at the dark hills. "Sit," she said. "Just for a bit."

qa.q: What did Dolma write in her status?
qa.a: She wrote a single line: 'some doors close quietly.'

qa.q: What might Dolma be feeling as she keeps running the drills?
qa.a: She is probably hurting and trying to outrun it through activity, and her cryptic status suggests she wants to be noticed without having to explain; another reading is that she simply needed exercise.

qa.q: What could Anirban do after she sits down?
qa.a: He can stay beside her, listen if she wants to talk, and let her go at her own pace without pushing for details.

qa.q: Why might Anirban have come with a torch rather than messaging her?
qa.a: He saw that she was still out in the dark and cold, and being physically there shows care that a message could not, especially when the phone signal is poor.

grounding: After a breakup or split a teen withdraws, posts a cryptic line and throws herself into activity, and a friend's support begins recovery.

passage: Counsellor's note. Mridul came to see me during the free period. He said his friend Sumit, usually the class joker, had been quiet for two weeks, yawning through lessons and missing the lunch table. Mridul had wondered whether to just leave it. Instead he sat next to Sumit on the bus and said, "How are you really?" Sumit answered that he was fine, then admitted he'd been sleeping badly because his family's shop had been struggling and everyone at home was tense. Mridul did not try to solve it. He listened, and then told me because he was a little worried. I thanked Mridul for both steps and arranged a quiet chat with Sumit for tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Mridul ask Sumit on the bus?
qa.a: He asked, 'How are you really?'

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: He felt a little worried, because Sumit's quietness, yawning and missing lunch had gone on for two weeks and Sumit's answer did not fully settle him.

qa.q: Why was telling the counsellor a sensible next step?
qa.a: Mridul could listen but couldn't fix a family problem, so passing on a real worry to a trusted adult was the right support for Sumit.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel about Mridul's question?
qa.a: He may feel relieved that someone noticed, though he first said he was fine, so he may also feel a little exposed.

grounding: A teen notices a friend who is quiet and tired, asks how he really is, and takes serious worry to a trusted adult.

passage: Thursday night. Sid barely laughed at any of my jokes today, and he didn't even fight me for the back seat on the bus. I didn't want to just guess, because I got it wrong last time when I thought he was angry with me. So at the bus stop I asked, "How are you really?" He blinked, then said he was tired and it was just the exams. I don't think that was the whole story, but he seemed glad I asked. He walked slowly home and didn't say goodbye the usual way. I'll ask him again on Saturday. If he still seems low then, I'm going to tell Mrs Nair, because I don't want to carry it alone. 🙂 - Manoj

qa.q: Where did Manoj ask Sid how he really was?
qa.a: Manoj asked at the bus stop.

qa.q: What does Manoj think about Sid's answer that it was just the exams?
qa.a: Manoj doesn't think it was the whole story, since Sid was quieter than usual and left without the usual goodbye, though he did seem glad to be asked.

qa.q: What will Manoj do if Sid still seems low on Saturday?
qa.a: Manoj plans to tell Mrs Nair, a trusted adult, so as not to carry the worry alone.

qa.q: How might Sid have felt when Manoj asked?
qa.a: He may have felt surprised and a bit relieved that someone noticed, even if he wasn't ready to say everything.

grounding: A teen diary shows reading a friend's quiet mood, asking gently, and planning to involve a trusted adult if worry continues.

passage: There were only ten minutes left before the project was due, and the group's laptop was slow. Rafiq suggested using a chart for the last slide. Vinita rolled her eyes, her lip curling slightly, and said, "Oh sure, because your ideas always work." A couple of others laughed uneasily. Rafiq felt heat rise in his face. He noticed the eye-roll wasn't about the chart; it said he wasn't worth hearing. He breathed in and said calmly, "When you roll your eyes like that, it feels like my ideas don't count. I'd like to keep working with you, but not like this." Vinita blinked. "I didn't mean it like that," she said, and the group went quiet, then turned back to the chart.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the project was due?
qa.a: Ten minutes were left before the project was due.

qa.q: What did Rafiq feel the eye-roll was saying about him?
qa.a: He read that it said he wasn't worth hearing, which hurt; although Vinita may only have been stressed by the deadline.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that helped in this moment?
qa.a: He named the effect calmly instead of retaliating, saying how the eye-roll felt and that he still wanted to work together.

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt after Rafiq spoke?
qa.a: She was probably taken aback and perhaps a little ashamed, since she said she didn't mean it that way, and her stress may have shown up as scorn.

grounding: A teen recognises an eye-roll and dismissive tone as contempt and responds by calmly naming its effect.

passage: Every evening the colony kids played cricket in the parking lot, and every evening Lalit had something to say. Today, when Chaitanya asked to bat, Lalit looked him up and down, gave a small twist of a smile, and said, "Oh, you're playing? Cute." Nobody laughed, but nobody objected either. Chaitanya felt the words land like a door shut in his face. It was the tone, not the bat, that told him he was beneath Lalit. He kept his voice level. "That sounded like you think I'm not good enough. It doesn't feel nice." Lalit shrugged and turned away. Chaitanya picked up his bat, took a breath, and walked home with his cousin, choosing not to stay where he felt small.

qa.q: Where did the colony kids play cricket?
qa.a: They played cricket in the parking lot.

qa.q: What did Lalit's tone make Chaitanya feel?
qa.a: He understood that Lalit thought he was beneath him, which felt like a door shut in his face, though nobody else said it aloud.

qa.q: Why might walking away have been a wise choice for Chaitanya?
qa.a: He named the effect calmly and Lalit didn't change, so leaving protected Chaitanya's dignity without starting a fight.

qa.q: How might the other kids have felt watching this?
qa.a: They may have felt uncomfortable and unsure whether to speak up, since no one laughed but no one objected either.

grounding: A teen reads contempt in a dismissive tone, names its effect calmly and chooses to leave when it doesn't change.

subtype: Defiant, irritated and frustrated with authority [Mismatch]
passage:
Monday. Ujjwal refused to go to evening tuition. When his father Kishore asked why, Ujjwal said, "Because I don't want to," slammed his bag on the sofa and stayed silent through dinner. Kishore felt his temper rise but held back.
Wednesday. Kishore sat beside him after supper and asked, "Something's off. What's going on?" After a pause, Ujjwal said he was exhausted by late nights of homework and dreaded the tutor calling him lazy in front of others.
Sunday. The two arranged an earlier session and a talk with the tutor. Ujjwal was still short-tempered sometimes, but he answered properly when spoken to.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal refuse to attend on Monday?
qa.a: He refused to attend evening tuition.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal be feeling underneath his sullen silence and backtalk?
qa.a: Exhaustion from late nights of homework and dread of being called lazy in front of others; his defiance also showed a wish to be heard.

qa.q: Why did asking before punishing help in this family?
qa.a: Kishore learned the real reasons, so they could change the timing and talk to the tutor, and the communication stayed open.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt when his father asked him calmly on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was probably relieved and surprised not to be punished, which made it easier to admit the real reasons.

grounding: A teenager's sullen silence and backtalk hide exhaustion and fear, and a parent who asks before punishing learns more.

subtype: Defiant, irritated and frustrated with authority [Mismatch]
passage: "You remind me of myself, Karthik," Asif said, watching his grandson push his food around. "At fifteen I answered every rule with a scowl. My father said be home by eight, I'd come at nine, arms folded, mouth shut." He laughed quietly. "People said I was rude. Really I wanted to be trusted. And I was scared about failing my board exams, and too proud to say it." Karthik looked up. "What did your father do?" "He could have shouted. Instead he asked me one evening, 'What's making you so angry?' I couldn't answer, but I remembered the asking. A month later, I told him everything." Asif stirred his tea. "Ask me, if you like. I won't punish first."

qa.q: What time did Asif's father want him home?
qa.a: His father said to be home by eight.

qa.q: What did Asif really want and fear at fifteen, behind the scowling?
qa.a: A wish to be trusted, along with fear of failing his board exams that he was too proud to say.

qa.q: What would you advise Karthik if he feels angry at rules?
qa.a: He could think about what is behind the anger, such as tiredness or worry, and take Asif up on the offer to talk.

qa.q: How might Asif's father have felt when his son came home late with folded arms?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated and worried, but choosing to ask what was making his son angry shows he wanted to understand first.

grounding: A teen's sullen defiance can mean fear and a wish for autonomy, and an adult who asks before punishing keeps communication open.

passage:
Dear Pema,
I know I slammed the door on you yesterday and left without a word. I want to explain. When you told the whole team about my wrong answer, everything in me went hot. My hands were shaking and I had no words, so I stormed off and then went silent for the rest of the day. I'm not proud of it. I walked around the block twice and breathed slowly until my chest loosened. By evening the anger had gone from a wave to a small ripple. I still think you shouldn't have said it in front of everyone, but I should have told you that instead of slamming things. Can we talk after school tomorrow?
Ira

qa.q: How did Ira behave right after Pema's comment?
qa.a: Ira stormed off and went silent for the rest of the day.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when Ira slammed the door, and how did it change?
qa.a: Ira was furious, with hot, shaking anger, and after walking and slow breathing it eased from a wave to a small ripple.

qa.q: What did Ira do that helped repair things with Pema?
qa.a: Ira stepped away, breathed until calm returned, and then wrote to explain and ask to talk, which protects the friendship.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt when the door slammed?
qa.a: Pema may have felt shocked or worried and perhaps a bit guilty, not knowing why Ira left, which is why the letter's explanation matters.

grounding: A teen's intense rage shows as slamming and silence, then fades after stepping away and breathing, and the teen returns to talk.

passage: Nazia, you asked about my worst temper day, so here it is. I'm Shreya. My little brother spilled water over my art project the night before submission. I didn't scream. I went completely cold and silent, and my brother kept saying sorry, but my jaw was locked and I walked past him like he wasn't there. Then I realised my hands were trembling. So I went up to the terrace and counted my breaths until my heart slowed down. It took a while. When I came back down, the fury had gone flat, and I saw he was sitting on the stairs looking miserable. I said, "I'm still upset, but I'm not angry at you as a person." We fixed the corners together.

qa.q: What did Shreya's brother spill over Shreya's art project?
qa.a: He spilled water over Shreya's art project the night before submission.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when going cold and silent?
qa.a: Shreya was furious, and the locked jaw and trembling hands show how strong it was, even though Shreya did not shout.

qa.q: What could Shreya do next time to protect the bond with the brother?
qa.a: Shreya could step away and breathe, then come back later and tell him calmly how it feels, as happened on the stairs.

qa.q: How might Shreya's brother have felt when Shreya walked past him?
qa.a: He probably felt guilty and scared, which is why he kept saying sorry and sat miserable on the stairs.

grounding: A teen with intense rage goes silent and cold, steps away to breathe, and returns to talk once it fades.

passage: On Friday, Aditi saw the senior by the staircase glaring at her. He stood in the middle of the landing, arms folded, and as she came closer he stepped sideways to block the way, sneering, "Where do you think you're going?" Her stomach tightened and her mouth went dry. She didn't answer back. She turned around, walked to the crowded corridor where her friend Ishita was, and said quietly, "Come with me to the staff room. Someone is blocking the stairs and I feel unsafe." Ishita didn't hesitate. They went together, and Aditi told the teacher on duty exactly what had happened, without exaggerating.

qa.q: Where did the senior block Aditi's way?
qa.a: He blocked her way on the landing by the staircase.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when the senior sneered at her?
qa.a: She felt unsafe and frightened, shown by the tight stomach and dry mouth, and she chose not to answer back.

qa.q: Why was going to a teacher with Ishita a wise choice?
qa.a: Hostility is a warning to disengage, stay near others and involve a trusted adult, not to retaliate.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt when Aditi asked Ishita to come along?
qa.a: Ishita may have felt worried for Aditi but also trusted, since Ishita went at once and gave support.

grounding: A teen notices a peer glaring and blocking the way, feels unsafe, and disengages, stays near others and tells a trusted adult.

passage:
"You look weird. What happened?" Rukmini said, putting down her book as Kamal dropped his bag in the hall.
"There's a boy at the cycle stand. He stares at me every day like he wants a fight. Today he stood in front of my cycle and wouldn't move."
"Did you say anything?"
"No. My hands were shaking. I wanted to shove him, honestly."
"Good that you didn't. Next time, stay near other people and don't wait around alone. And tell your class teacher today, not next week."
"Won't that make it worse?"
"Maybe he'll be embarrassed. Maybe not. But you shouldn't handle this by yourself." She squeezed his shoulder. "I'll come to school with you tomorrow if you like."

qa.q: Where does the boy stare at Kamal every day?
qa.a: He stares at Kamal at the cycle stand.

qa.q: What does Kamal's wish to shove the boy suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests fear mixed with anger, since his hands were shaking, but he held back.

qa.q: What would you advise Kamal to do first?
qa.a: Tell his class teacher today and stay near other people, as Rukmini says, instead of retaliating or handling it alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini to hear this?
qa.a: She is probably worried and protective, which is why she offers to go to school with him. 🙂

grounding: A teen faces a peer glaring and blocking his way and is advised to disengage, stay near others and involve a trusted adult.

subtype: Apologetic and pleading in peer conflict [Interpreting]
passage: Counsellor's note. Ira came to see me about her friend Pema, who had shared one of Ira's private messages with the group. Since then Pema has sent a quick "sorry" each morning, and last night she wrote, "please please forgive me, I'll do anything." Ira said her voice in person is soft and shaky, and Ira didn't know whether to believe it. She also felt pressure from other friends to make up quickly. We talked about how sincerity is usually clear from what someone does differently as weeks pass, not from how loudly someone says sorry, and that Ira is allowed to say she needs space. I suggested she wait and watch what Pema does next. We will meet again next week.

qa.q: What had Pema shared with the group?
qa.a: Pema shared one of Ira's private messages with the group.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling about Pema's apologies?
qa.a: She was unsure whether to believe them, since the sorries were quick and the begging text was intense; she also felt pressure from other friends.

qa.q: What could Ira do while she decides whether to forgive?
qa.a: She can say she needs space and watch whether Pema's behaviour changes over time.

qa.q: How might Pema feel while sending so many apologies?
qa.a: She may feel anxious and truly regretful, or afraid of losing the friendship, though the messages alone can't prove which.

grounding: A teen reads a friend's quick sorry and begging texts, and learns sincerity shows over time and forgiveness needn't be forced.

subtype: Apologetic and pleading in peer conflict [Interpreting]
passage: Tuesday. Gautam has texted "sorry" again and again since Sunday, and today he wrote, "I can't sleep, please say something." My stomach twists every time my phone buzzes. Part of me wants to forgive him, because he sounds so upset. But he did the same after he skipped our practice last month, promised to change, and then did it again. So I'm not sure the sorry is a lie; it just doesn't tell me much yet. Anita said I'm being harsh. I told her I'm not being harsh, I'm just not ready. I'll reply tomorrow with one line: I need time, and I'll see how you act. - Jaya

qa.q: What did Gautam write today?
qa.a: He wrote, 'I can't sleep, please say something.'

qa.q: Why is Jaya hesitant to forgive Gautam right away?
qa.a: He apologised and promised to change last month and then did it again, so his sorry alone doesn't tell Jaya much, even though part of Jaya wants to forgive.

qa.q: What does Jaya plan to say to Gautam, and why does it help?
qa.a: Jaya plans to ask for time and will see how he acts, which sets a boundary and lets his behaviour speak.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel while Jaya stays silent?
qa.a: He may feel anxious and desperate for reassurance, but that pressure is not a reason for Jaya to give in before feeling ready.

grounding: A teen reads a friend's begging texts, doubts their sincerity until behaviour changes, and keeps a boundary.

passage: I'm Joseph, and I live next door to my cousin Reena's family, so I see a lot. On Sunday Reena took her friend's earrings home from the sleepover and lost one. When her mother asked about it at the gate, Reena went red and hid in her room for hours. I could hear her say, "I'm such a rubbish person." At dinner she barely spoke. Her mother didn't shout. She said, "You made a mistake with the earring, but you're not rubbish. What could you do about it?" Reena went quiet. I honestly can't tell if she was ashamed or just embarrassed. Next morning she wrote a note to her friend and offered to buy a new pair.

qa.q: What did Reena lose after the sleepover?
qa.a: She lost one of her friend's earrings.

qa.q: What did Reena's words 'I'm such a rubbish person' suggest?
qa.a: They suggest shame, feeling bad as a person and not only about the act, though Joseph can't be sure how deep it went.

qa.q: What did Reena's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She separated the mistake from Reena as a person and asked what she could do about it, which turned hiding into repair.

qa.q: How does Joseph's view differ from what Reena is feeling inside?
qa.a: Joseph only sees the red face, the hiding and the note, so guilt and shame look alike to Joseph, who admits being unable to tell them apart.

grounding: A teen's guilt (I did something bad) and shame (I am bad) look alike from outside; care for the person turns hiding into repair.

passage:
Day 1. Urmila forgot to submit the group science project, and Darshan, her partner, lost marks with her. She stayed in her room, refused dinner and told her aunt, "I ruin everything."
Day 3. Her aunt sat on the bed and said, "Forgetting the file was a mistake. That doesn't make you a bad partner or a bad person. What could you fix?" Urmila stayed quiet, wiping her eyes, then whispered that she'd let Darshan down.
Day 6. Urmila messaged Darshan, said sorry without excuses, and offered to redo the whole report with him. Darshan replied, "Okay, Saturday at the library?" She finally smiled.

qa.q: What did Urmila forget to submit?
qa.a: She forgot to submit the group science project.

qa.q: What might Urmila be feeling when she says 'I ruin everything'?
qa.a: Shame, the feeling that she is bad as a person, not just guilt about the file; hiding in her room fits that.

qa.q: How did her aunt help Urmila move from hiding to repair?
qa.a: She separated the mistake from the person and asked what Urmila could fix, so the shame eased and repair became possible.

qa.q: How might Darshan have felt when Urmila offered to redo the report?
qa.a: He was probably relieved and willing to forgive, since he suggested a time at the library straight away.

grounding: A teen slides from 'I did something bad' to 'I am bad', and care for the person turns hiding into repair.

passage: Yamini was picked to read out the group's poem in Hindi class, and I sat two seats from her, so I watched the whole thing. When Sir called her name, she went red from neck to forehead and looked at her paper as if it might rescue her. She spoke so softly the back row shouted "Louder!" Her voice shook, but she didn't stop. Then she gave a tiny laugh and read the last two lines with her hand covering half her face. At the break she told me she had rehearsed it in front of the mirror all week. I can't tell if she hated every second or secretly liked it. - Ramesh

qa.q: What did the back row shout at Yamini?
qa.a: The back row shouted 'Louder!'

qa.q: What might Yamini be feeling as she reads, and what else might be true?
qa.a: She is likely embarrassed and self-conscious, shown by her blushing and covering her face; she may also feel proud, since she kept going and had rehearsed all week.

qa.q: What small step could help Yamini feel more comfortable next time?
qa.a: She could read to one or two friends first, then to a small group, building comfort in tiny steps.

qa.q: How might the back row's shout have felt to Yamini?
qa.a: It may have added to her worry about how she seemed, or it may have felt like ordinary classroom noise; she could not easily tell which.

grounding: A shy teen blushes, avoids the spotlight and overthinks how she seems; small steps build comfort.

passage:
Day 1. Ayesha stood at the door of the drama club room, then walked past it. Her friend Keerthana had asked her to try a session, but Ayesha imagined everyone staring at her and left for the library.
Day 5. Keerthana said, "Just sit at the back with me. You don't have to do anything." Ayesha went, sat quietly, and her ears burned when the teacher glanced at her, but nobody paid attention.
Day 12. During a warm-up circle, Ayesha said her name and one favourite food, in a tiny voice. People clapped once and moved on. She walked home feeling lighter than she had in weeks.

qa.q: Where did Ayesha go instead of the drama club on day one?
qa.a: She went to the library.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha walk past the drama club room on day one?
qa.a: She imagined everyone staring at her, which reflects the self-consciousness that keeps her from going in.

qa.q: How did Keerthana make it easier for Ayesha to join in?
qa.a: Keerthana offered a small step, sitting at the back together with no pressure to do anything, so comfort could grow gradually.

qa.q: How might the other club members have seen Ayesha's tiny voice?
qa.a: They probably saw it as an ordinary introduction and clapped once before moving on, so it felt much bigger to her than to them.

grounding: A shy teen avoids the spotlight and builds comfort through small steps into a social situation.

passage: "Your Uncle Suresh does it too," Manjula told Shreya, pointing at her granddaughter's hand. "Nodding at me with his eyes on that phone. I used to think he was listening because his head kept bobbing." She tucked a cushion behind her back. "One day I was telling him about my knee doctor's appointment, and he said, 'Mm-hm, sure,' and then asked me to repeat everything. I wasn't cross. It was only that I couldn't tell from the nodding." Shreya set down her phone. "What did you do?" "I asked him one small question: 'Can you tell me what I said last?' We both laughed, and after that he put the phone face down when I began."

qa.q: What was Manjula telling Uncle Suresh about?
qa.a: She was telling him about her knee doctor's appointment.

qa.q: What does Suresh's nodding show about his attention?
qa.a: It doesn't prove he was listening, since his head kept bobbing while his eyes stayed on the phone; he might have been half-listening.

qa.q: What could Shreya try if she isn't sure someone is listening to her?
qa.a: She could ask a brief question such as 'What did I say last?' to check gently, instead of assuming.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt when Suresh asked her to repeat everything?
qa.a: She may have felt a little unheard, though she says she wasn't cross, and she chose a light question rather than a complaint.

grounding: A teen nodding while looking at a phone may or may not be listening, and a brief question checks it.

passage: The metro platform was loud with announcements and rush-hour footsteps, and Vidya had to raise her voice to be heard. She was telling Raghav about her audition, one of the most important things in her month. Raghav nodded along, murmuring "yeah, yeah," but his eyes kept dropping to his phone in his hand. Vidya couldn't tell whether he was really with her or waiting for a message. She wasn't sure the noise had let her words through at all. She stopped mid-sentence and said, "Sorry, it's so loud. Did you catch that last part, or should I pause?" Raghav looked up, startled. "Honestly, I'm waiting for my cab to be confirmed. Tell me again, I'm listening now."

qa.q: Where were Vidya and Raghav standing?
qa.a: They were on the metro platform.

qa.q: What was Vidya worried about as Raghav nodded?
qa.a: She wasn't sure whether he was really with her or waiting for a message, since nodding and glancing at a phone don't show attention on their own.

qa.q: What did Vidya do that helped clear things up?
qa.a: She asked a brief, friendly question, checking if he had caught the last part, instead of guessing or getting annoyed.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when Vidya stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: He was probably startled and a little caught out, but honest, since he explained that he was waiting for his cab and asked her to repeat it.

grounding: A teen nodding while glancing at a phone may be listening or elsewhere, and a brief question checks attention.
